rv.q: Max Webster's production of Life Of Pi has weathered better; and is now, quite simply, a wonder to behold.

There’s a philosophical thread to what unfolds. The fable asks big questions about how we can prove our version of events, the value of storytelling and our capacity to believe extraordinary things because we sense the world is strange beyond measure.
But for theatregoers looking for a new dimension in puppetry and storytelling, this tale of fur and fortitude is just amazing.
This stage version of Yann Martel’s Booker Prize winner has to stand as one of the most visually stunning theatre shows I’ve ever seen, especially in the feverishly beautiful second half...
As a children's show, the jokes hold but an older audience feels the lack of a finer, more subtle script to square up to the sophisticated visuals.
'Life of Pi' is fantastical, and director Max Webster's extraordinary West End production is fantastic.
This amazing technical achievement should be seen, and marvelled at, by anyone with an interest in making stage scenery.
Otherwise, this is a gorgeous staging by adaptor Lolita Chakrabarti and director Max Webster: vivid, witty, poignant and wondrous.

As the production unfolds there is much to love, but its astonishing power comes from the puppetry, which is overseen by Finn Caldwell who has a pedigree that goes back to the National Theatre’s War Horse.

Life of Pi is a sumptuous, visual treat for the senses, a remarkably vivid recreation of a classic novel, and an effective reminder that sometimes the stories we tell ourselves are stronger than the truth.
It's a wonder and I wanted to love it whole-heartedly.

For those who were captivated and engrossed by Yann Martel’s 2001 award winning novel, the stage adaptation will tick most of the plot boxes and mesmerise through sheer technical invention, but the production itself fails to genuinely engage on an emotional level.
Having seen it, I feel luckier still.
